title: Hōkūleʻa voyage from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti
summary: Hōkūleʻa, a double-hulled voyaging canoe built by the Polynesian Voyaging Society, was launched at Honolua Bay, Maui, on 1 May 1976 and reached Tahiti on 4 June without modern navigation instruments. Micronesian master navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal guided it by traditional wayfinding, and more than 17,000 people welcomed the canoe at Papeete.

uncertainty.note: Dates from the Hawaii House resolution and Ben Finney's account; the canoe sailed back to Hawaiʻi afterwards (return voyage not covered here). Sources differ on days at sea (34 in the resolution; 30 to Mataiva in Finney).

as_recorded.value: launched at Honolua Bay, Maui, on May 1, 1976 ... reached Tahiti safely on June 4, 1976

importance.justification: A navigation by traditional wayfinding from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti that the Hawaii legislature credits with rekindling appreciation of Polynesian voyaging.

reviewer_note: Honolua point is Wikidata's "area in West Maui", not the bay mouth; Mataiva is the atoll centre. The crowd figure of more than 17,000 is given on the Finney page as Nainoa Thompson's statement. Other sources give 3 June for arrival; both opened pages say 4 June. Piailug is described by the resolution as a traditional master navigator from Satawal, Micronesia, chosen because no present-day Polynesians knew the ancient methods.

beats.caption: Hōkūleʻa leaves Honolua Bay, Maui, under master navigator Mau Piailug, using wayfinding without compass or sextant.
After weeks at sea the canoe makes landfall at Mataiva atoll in French Polynesia.
More than 17,000 people greet the canoe at Papeete; the Hawaii legislature credits the voyage with renewing appreciation of Polynesian navigation.
